items.question: Which ideal body weight formula is most accurate?
items.answer: No single formula is definitively most accurate  -  they are all approximations from different historical datasets. The Devine formula is most commonly used in clinical medicine for drug dosing. The Hamwi formula is popular among dietitians. For personal health purposes a healthy BMI range (18.5 to 24.9) combined with waist circumference measurement provides a more complete picture than any single IBW formula.

items.question: Is ideal body weight the same as healthy weight?
items.answer: Not exactly. IBW formulas produce a single number while healthy weight is better understood as a range. The healthy BMI range of 18.5 to 24.9 typically encompasses the IBW estimates from most formulas. IBW also does not account for body composition  -  a person can be at their IBW but have an unhealthy ratio of fat to muscle.

items.question: What if I am shorter than 5 feet?
items.answer: Most standard IBW formulas become unreliable below 5 feet in height because they were derived from populations with limited representation of shorter adults. For people under 5 feet, BMI-based healthy weight ranges are generally more appropriate, though even these have limitations. Consult a healthcare provider for personalised guidance.

items.question: Can your ideal body weight change over time?
items.answer: The IBW formulas do not change with age since they are based solely on height. However what constitutes a healthy weight in practice may shift with age  -  particularly in older adults where maintaining muscle mass becomes more important and some additional weight may be associated with better outcomes. Standard IBW formulas should be interpreted with age in mind.

items.question: How is ideal body weight used in medicine?
items.answer: The most important clinical use of IBW is medication dosing. Many drugs  -  particularly antibiotics, anaesthetic agents, and chemotherapy  -  are dosed based on IBW rather than actual body weight because the drug distributes through lean tissue rather than fat. Using actual weight for these medications in obese patients would result in overdosing.
